And perhaps that was the entirety of the blessing that could ever be given by two people who both could never speak: not words, in the end, but presence—one afternoon, then another afternoon, in a cramped shop, among fabric and thread and a chessboard with a button king, two men guarding each other from the exact same silence, one who forgot and one who finally, belatedly, chose to stay.
Outside, the afternoon slowly descended upon the narrow alley. Inside, the old man moved his piece, and lost, and chuckled, and said to the stranger he cared for without knowing why:
"Come again tomorrow, okay, son. I'm happy to have a friend."
And Banyu, who his entire life left, said the thing he his entire life never said to anyone, and this time he said it, and this time he would keep it:
"Yes, Sir. Tomorrow I'll come again."

sides.title: The Woman Who Counted Backwards
body: The first thing Maryam counted was the spoons. It was the fourth morning of her marriage. She opened the kitchen drawer in their new house and counted the teaspoons—twelve, in pairs, a gift from someone or other—and felt, for a reason she couldn't explain, relieved. Twelve was a full number. Even. Enough for guests who hadn't arrived, children who hadn't been born, years that hadn't been lived. She closed the drawer and didn't think about it again for years.

She didn't know, that morning, that she would spend the rest of her marriage counting. That counting would become her way of surviving, then her way of tormenting herself, then the only language left to measure something that had no units. She just closed the drawer, and brewed tea for two, and waited for her husband to come down.

Saman proposed to her without words. He sewed Maryam a dress—secretly, with measurements he somehow knew exactly—and handed it over with eyes that didn't dare lift from the floor. Maryam understood that the dress was a proposal, because the man had no sentences to propose with, and she accepted.

At twenty-two, she thought a man's silence was depth. She thought behind a person who didn't talk much there must be something massive, stored away, waiting for the one right person to open it up. She thought she would be that person.

She wasn't completely wrong. There was something massive behind Saman's silence. Maryam spent ten years trying to reach it, and found that the massive thing was real—she saw it, sometimes, in her husband's eyes, something full and urgent and clearly wanting to get out. But there was no way there. Not a locked door. Something worse: a wall built so neatly that even the one inside forgot there used to be a door.

She couldn't hate Saman, and that was what was most exhausting. If Saman were abusive, she would have a reason, and a reason is a grip. But Saman was gentle. He saved the best cut on the plate for Maryam. He sewed Maryam the most beautiful clothes in town, which Maryam wore to parties where other women praised her and told her how lucky she was, how attentive her husband was, and Maryam smiled and agreed and went home to a silent house and felt like a liar.

Because no one believes in the loneliness of a woman who has everything. It is a loneliness you have to deny every day, until the denial itself becomes a full-time job, until you forget which is you and which is your denial.
She counted sentences. It was a habit that grew without her deciding to.

Not sentences like "where's the salt" or "close the shop, it's going to rain". The other sentences—sentences that mentioned feelings, that mentioned Maryam as Maryam and not as part of the household machinery. Some days she got one. Most days, zero.

She hoarded those numbers the way people hoard debts. And she hated herself for counting—because counting means measuring, and measuring someone's love is a small betrayal against them, and Saman didn't deserve to be betrayed even secretly, even just inside her head. But she couldn't stop. Numbers were the only way she could prove to herself that what she felt was real, that she wasn't crazy, that the emptiness she felt wasn't her fabrication—because if she could count it, she existed.

And this was what she didn't admit until years later: that Saman, perhaps, was also counting. That on the other side of the same wall, there was a man who was also measuring something he feared was insufficient, who was also hoarding numbers, who also felt like a liar at parties. That two people could live in one house, love sincerely, and each be convinced they were the only one who was lonely. Maryam never asked him about it. It was among the things she never asked, and that non-asking, she understood now, was the first brick of her own wall.
Then Banyu was born, and for a few years Maryam thought she was saved.

A baby is a creature full of sounds, full of demands, full of mouths that must be fed and eyes that light up when you enter a room. Maryam poured into her son all the words that had no place to go for ten years. She talked to Banyu all day long, even when the child was too small to understand, because finally there was someone listening.
But a child is not a vessel you can fill limitlessly without consequences. And one day, when Banyu was seven or eight, Maryam heard herself do something that made her hand stop mid-stir.

Banyu fell, scraped his knee, and cried. And Maryam, instead of asking "does it hurt?", found herself saying: "There, stop crying. It's okay. Hush." With a gentle voice. With a voice that was exactly—exactly—the voice used to muffle, to shut down, to teach a child that feelings are something better left unseen.
Her husband's voice. Coming out of her own mouth.

She stood in the kitchen with a spoon in her hand and realized she had been wrong all along. She thought Saman was silencing her. But silence, it turned out, didn't come from one direction and stay there; it spread, it was contagious, it entered the people living nearby and came out through their mouths without permission. Ten years beside a wall had made Maryam into a bit of a wall herself. And now that wall was building itself, brick by brick, around her eight-year-old son, through her own hands, through her own voice, through her own love.
That was the thing that finally made her decide to leave. Not her loneliness—she had already learned to bear her loneliness. But the horror of seeing herself pass it down.
I want to pause here for a moment, because this is the part you must know, and there is no clean way to say it.
Maryam left a nine-year-old child.

There is no paragraph that can make that painless. There is no excuse noble enough to make a child who wakes up and finds his mother gone feel less abandoned. Whatever Maryam thought she was saving by leaving, there is a boy who will grow up with a mother-shaped hole in his chest, who will check the mailbox for twelve years, who will hate something he doesn't understand until his hatred hardens into bone. Maryam knew this. She knew this the morning she left, and she knew this every morning after, and there wasn't a single day in the long rest of her life when she successfully completely convinced herself that she had been right.

That was what made her different from her husband, in the end. Not that she spoke and Saman was silent. But that Maryam carried her doubts with her, for a lifetime, open, incurable—while Saman buried his in a drawer. They both did damage. It was just that one refused to pretend the damage wasn't there.

Should she have stayed? I don't know. Maryam didn't know. Maybe staying would have made her a ghost, and made Banyu a child raised by a ghost, and made Banyu's future wife marry a ghost—a polite lineage of loneliness, straight down, unbroken. Or maybe that was just a story she fabricated to bear what she had already done. Maybe both are true. Maybe a decision can save someone and destroy someone else with the exact same action, and we are given no way to separate the two, and we still have to choose.
Maryam chose. And she paid for her choice every day until she died. That is not a justification. That is just what happened.
On the morning she left, she stood for a long time in her sleeping son's room.

She tried to wake him up. She swore she tried. There were entire paragraphs in her chest—paragraphs about the kitchen, about the wall, about why, about sorry—and she opened her mouth to speak them, and found, at the moment she needed it most, that her mouth closed.

Exactly like her husband's mouth at the shop door, years later, when that same boy would leave with a backpack on his back. Exactly like that boy's mouth, years further on, at the apartment door, when a woman named Sari would lift a suitcase. The same family. The same disease. And Maryam, who left precisely to break that chain, found herself at the final moment becoming just one more link in it—mute beside the person she most wanted to talk to.

So she wrote. Hands, sometimes, can do what mouths cannot. But even on paper her courage was only enough for a few lines—a tenth of what was in her chest, because a dam doesn't collapse just because you hand it a pen. She wrote a short note. She placed it on the kitchen table, under a cup, next to the drawer where twelve spoons now lived as eleven—because she took one, that morning, one teaspoon, without knowing why, perhaps just so there would be something from this house coming with her, something small and even and once full.
Then she kissed her son's forehead, very softly so as not to wake him—because if Banyu opened his eyes and looked at her, she knew she wouldn't have the strength to step outside—and she left.

That note never reached Banyu. Saman found it first, read it, and hid it. Not to protect his son. To protect himself—because among those short lines, Maryam had written a sentence about loving someone from a place she couldn't reach, and that sentence was a mirror Saman couldn't bear to face. So he buried it in the same drawer where he would later bury his own unsent letters. And his son grew up hating a silence, never knowing that the silence had once, a single time, tried to speak.

The world never asks what happens to the women who leave. Once the door closes, she ceases to exist; she becomes a hole in someone else's house, an absence shaped like a mother, an empty chair that other people stare at while wondering. But she didn't stop existing.
Maryam fled to a distant port city. A city that smelled of salt, fish guts, and ship oil.

The first few years were a brutal physical torment. She worked washing dishes at a stall by the pier. The wet and cold sea wind gnawed at her body. One night, she was struck by a severe fever for days. An infection attacked her left ear because it went untreated. When her fever broke, half of Maryam's world had become soundproof. She was officially half deaf.
Her hair turned white prematurely. Her back began to hunch from exhaustion. In her late thirties, her face wrinkled like a woman in her fifties.
She later worked for an old, nearly blind watch repairman, learning to disassemble and assemble gears and springs. When the owner died, Maryam inherited that small, dark shop.

Maryam liked watches. In that shop, hundreds of watches ticked simultaneously. That noisy *tick-tock* drowned out the silence that used to choke her in Saman's house. In the corner of her workbench, Maryam placed an empty glass bottle plugged with a cork. Every time she felt her chest tighten from missing Banyu, she didn't cry; she picked up a broken gear, and dropped it into the glass bottle. Saving a minute of her suffering, locking it up tightly.
Eight years after her flight, on a windy afternoon, her watch shop's door chime rang.

A teenage boy entered. He was perhaps barely seventeen. His clothes were shabby, and he carried a backpack soiled with street dust. He stood stiffly in front of the display case, his jaw clenched, his eyes staring down at the tiled floor.
"Can I help you, Son?" Maryam asked, tilting her head so her functioning right ear could hear.
"I need a job," the boy answered. His voice was low, hoarse, and restrained, as if he weren't used to using his vocal cords. "I can sweep, tidy the shelves. Anything."

Maryam looked at him for a long time. This port city was always full of wandering children running away from something. Every time she saw them, Maryam's chest throbbed with pain, because she always imagined Banyu. *This boy is the same age as Banyu now,* Maryam thought inwardly. She nodded, pointed to the broom in the corner of the room, and gave him a sleeping spot on a mat in the back storage room.
The boy was quiet. Very quiet.

He swept the floor almost without a sound. He ate his lunch rations in the corner of the room, always refusing to meet Maryam's eyes. Sometimes, when Maryam was hunched over installing a desk clock's gears, she glanced at the boy from behind her glasses. There was something in the boy that made Maryam's breath catch often. The way the boy stood with tense shoulders, the way he folded the dust cloth... somehow, those stiff movements evoked Maryam's memories of the way her husband held his fabric measuring tape in the past.

*This wandering boy must be running from a very cold house,* Maryam thought sympathetically, seeing how the boy locked himself away from the outside world. That thought made her haunted by a tremendous fear. *Is Banyu out there also drifting aimlessly like this boy? Is Banyu also freezing and building the same walls?*

Driven by her endless guilt towards her own biological son, Maryam tried to pour her attention into the quiet boy. Every Sunday, when the shop was closed, Maryam purposely cooked extra rice and side dishes.
"Eat with me, Son," Maryam called warmly from the wooden table in the back room, patting the empty chair next to her.

But the boy always froze in place. His face tensed as if kindness were something that threatened him. He shook his head stiffly, looked away, then stepped out of the shop and walked off to who-knows-where until late at night.

Every time the boy refused her dinner, Maryam swallowed her own food with an aching throat. The rejection slapped her. *Is this what it feels like to be ignored?* Maryam thought bitterly. *Is this what it feels like to stare at the back of someone who decides not to let you in?*
Six months the boy worked for her.
Then, one morning in the rainy season, Maryam awoke to a peculiar instinct. She walked slowly to the back storage room. The door was slightly ajar. The mat was empty. The shabby backpack was gone.
Maryam stood paralyzed at the threshold of the storage room. The dawn air blew in, bringing a cold chill. The boy had left. Secretly. Without saying goodbye.

Maryam walked unsteadily to the front desk. On the workbench where the boy usually organized the watches, she saw a banana leaf parcel. It was the rice and side dishes Maryam had woken up even earlier to cook, purposely placed there because she knew, from the look in the boy's eyes last night, that the boy was preparing to run away.

Maryam touched the banana leaf parcel that was slowly beginning to turn cold. The boy didn't take it. The boy rejected her offering until the very end. Refusing to have any ties whatsoever in this city.
Suddenly, Maryam's legs gave out. She slumped to the dusty wooden floor. Hugging her knees, Maryam cried without a sound until her entire chest convulsed.

The world truly knew how to punish her. Twelve years ago, she left the house before dawn, refusing to wake anyone, only leaving something on the table. Now, the universe forced her to feel the exact same pain, placing her precisely in the position of the one left behind.

In the midst of her agonizing sobs, Maryam's tears fell for Banyu. *Banyu... are you out there growing up into a boy this hard? Did you also leave the people who tried to care for you, exactly like this wandering boy left me?*

Maryam crawled to her workbench. With hands shaking violently, she opened the drawer, took out the cork-stoppered glass bottle, and dropped a broken metal gear into it. One minute full of regret, locked tightly at the bottom of the bottle.
Years passed since the nameless boy left. Maryam grew increasingly frail. Her hands were no longer strong enough to hold watch tweezers.

On a quiet morning, when she was in her extreme twilight years, Maryam sat near the open window of her shop. She took a piece of paper. She didn't know where Banyu was now, but she had to free this one thing from her chest.
She wrote slowly:

*Son. I will not explain why I left, because an explanation is just my way of asking you to understand, and you don't owe me any understanding. I just want you to know one small thing. I still remember your hand. Your little hand gripping the edge of the blanket when you slept. I left taking one teaspoon from our kitchen, and I still have it now. Every morning, when I stir my tea, I remember your hand.*

Maryam stopped writing for a moment. Her eyes gazed far off, staring at the empty workbench in the corner of the room, the place where that mute wandering boy once rejected all her attention. The sting of that dawn parting returned to disturb her.
Maryam swallowed hard, then added one final sentence into her letter:

*Out there, if there is someone who tries to offer you dinner or gives you shelter, please accept it, Son. Don't push them away. Don't let your heart turn to stone like the walls in our house used to be.*

She folded the letter. She wrote the address she had tracked down over the years through distant relatives and luck. She limped to the post office, sent it to her old, obsolete address, surrendering everything to fate. Calling out and being answered are two different things. Her only task was to call.

That afternoon, Maryam went home to her shop. She brewed hot tea in a glass cup. She took the 12th teaspoon—the spoon that once accompanied her in running away—and stirred her drink slowly. *Ting-ting-ting.* The sound of metal clinking against glass.

She sat smiling, watching hundreds of watches ticking. On the backmost shelf, the glass bottle filled with broken metal gears stood dusty. That morning, for the first time since the fourth morning of her marriage, she was no longer counting her mistakes. She took a deep breath, inhaling the morning air that smelled of sea salt, and for the first time, she felt even.

Maryam passed away peacefully in that chair during the following rainy season. She left carrying her peaceful ignorance. The shop was bequeathed with odd rules, but the dusty glass bottle on the back shelf remained untouched, guarding the frozen minutes, waiting patiently until over a decade later—when the shop's bell rang again, and a wandering man stepped in from the street, only to buy a dead pocket watch, and walked right past the single most precious minute of his own mother without ever knowing it.

title: Di Dasar Rumah
excerpt: Pada suatu masa di pedalaman desa yang indah, musim selalu datang dengan lembut. Musim seminya menyemai keindahan, sementara panasnya meneduhkan—hanya sesekali membuat peluh turun malu-malu…
body: Pada suatu masa di pedalaman desa yang indah, musim selalu datang dengan lembut. Musim seminya menyemai keindahan, sementara panasnya meneduhkan—hanya sesekali membuat peluh turun malu-malu dari wajah penduduknya. Begitupun dinginnya menenangkan serta merehatkan penduduknya sejenak tuk menikmati hasil kerja kerasnya. Saat itu musim-musim enggan merepotkan penduduknya, datangnya perlahan dan seolah bersiul lewat kilat kecil di ujung malam menandakan kerlipan musim yang akan berganti. Tepat dibawahnya, hiduplah seorang gadis manis penuh kehangatan meski dengan tangannya yang selalu dingin. Menatap penuh harap, berdoa barangkali. Agar hidupnya penuh dengan memori indah.

Namun, musim-musim yang ramah itu seolah berhenti di depan pintu rumah besar yang kini perlahan lapuk. Di dalamnya, gadis belia itu harus menghitung angka yang cukup merepotkannya — baginya memang banyak, banyak sekali, banyak yang membuatnya menghitung ulang di atas kertas sampai tiga kali untuk memastikan ia tidak salah membaca jumlah nol. Sejenak gadis itu menghela nafas panjang sembari menggosok-gosokan kedua tangannya, saat itu musim dingin yang menusuk. Dari helaan nafasnya bahkan membentuk kepulan uap tipis. Aneh pikirnya, tak biasanya musim dingin sedikit bermain kejam.

Pikirannya terasa menggema di rumah yang terlalu besar untuk dihangatkan, membuat suasana semakin menusuk. Besarnya rumah ini tidak lagi menjamin kemakmurannya sekarang, karena mereka terlalu miskin untuk memperbaikinya kembali. Dan sejak kecil ia belajar bahwa dingin bukanlah sesuatu yang dilawan, melainkan sesuatu yang ditemani, seperti adik yang sakit-sakitan yang tak mungkin kau benci walau ia membuatmu lelah.

Lalu gadis itu mengerutkan sedikit dahinya sembari memelintir ujung rambutnya yang hitam kecoklatan. Udara dingin menggigit kulit wajahnya yang kemerahan, seketika dia menggosokkan wajahnya dengan kedua tangannya seraya menggerutu kecil.
“Kenapa dunia menawariku dunia yang bisa diukur. Bukannya dunia yang bisa diingat”

Lalu gadis itu kembali tepekur dalam pikirannya. Memutar-mutar pena yang hampir kehabisan tinta karena sering ia buang tuk menghitung angka. Baginya dunia tak lebih dari angka, dan ia kecewa akan hal itu. Tidak, bukan karena gadis itu merasa direpotkan akan semua angka ini. Tapi ia begitu takut kenangan indahnya tergantikan oleh angka yang bermunculan satu persatu.

Tagihan tabib-tabib dari dalam dan luar desa adalah angka. Sisa hutang kebutuhan rumah adalah angka. Hari-hari Ibu yang tersisa, kata hampir semua tabib, entah terasa semacam angka — meski tak ada yang berani menuliskannya secara terang terangan.

Meski semua hal ini membebani pikiran sang gadis. Namun satu hal yang ia ingat. Ibunya menghangatkan tangan gadis itu dengan napasnya setiap pagi, dan setiap pagi berkata hal yang sama: *Tidurlah, nyala kecil, biar Ibu yang berjaga.* Dan sang gadis tersenyum dalam keadaan setengah terbangun seraya merayakan mimpi-mimpi yang ia mimpikan sebelumnya. Mereka berdua tertawa dan gadis itu kembali tidur dengan senyum kecil.

Lalu pada suatu pagi ibunya tidak bangun lagi. Jam di dinding masih berdetak, tetapi tidak ada lagi yang bernapas di kamar itu. Dan tidak ada lagi yang menghangatkan tangan gadis itu, dan rumah yang besar itu menjadi sedingin yang selalu ia takutkan. Bukan hanya ia menjadi sebatang kara, namun juga memori itu entah dalam angka keberapa akan menghilang. Gadis itu selalu memikirkan itu, selalu.

Maka ketika di sore yang hampir menyingsing, seorang perempuan bertopi datang mengetuk — perempuan yang wajahnya teduh seperti sore, yang suaranya seperti selimut — gadis itu membuka pintu perlahan, ia baru saja merajut pakaian tetangga, tentu dengan upah.
"Aku dengar," kata perempuan itu, "kau pandai menemani yang dingin."
"Aku tidak pandai apa-apa," balas gadis itu dengan dingin.

"Itulah kepandaian yang kumaksud," kata perempuan itu, dan tersenyum. "Aku punya pekerjaan untukmu, sayang. Pekerjaan yang hangat. Di dasar rumahku ada sebuah kamar, dan di kamar itu ada sebuah nyala kecil, dan nyala itu tidak boleh padam. Tugasmu hanya menjaganya. Duduk di sampingnya, dan menyayanginya, dan tidak membiarkannya tidur. Sebagai gantinya kau tidak akan pernah dingin lagi, dan ibumu" — perempuan itu menyentuh pipi gadis itu, dan tangannya hangat, hangat sekali — "ibumu akan tenang di tempat ia berada, karena utang-utang yang ditinggalkannya akan kuhapus, seolah-olah tak pernah ada.

Gadis itu terdiam sejenak. Memikirkan segala kerepotan yang telah di buat oleh angka-angka itu. Ia ingat pernah ada seseorang menjanjikan hal yang sama, namun seseorang itu sangat bau mulutnya dan wajahnya tidak enak dipandang. Lemak bergelambir di bawah dagu, ditangan, di perut, dan di segala tempat yang mungkin tak terpikirkan orang lain, ia yakin seseorang itu adalah manusia lemak. Gadis itu tidak mengerti mengapa ada orang lain yang rela repot repot membayarkan angka yang bahkan ia sendiri kerepotan karenanya. Namun ketika ia melihat sekali lagi nafas berat seseorang yang berlemak itu menggebu dan mungkin…. panas. Ia mengurungkan menerima tawaran itu dan menutup pintunya dengan keras.

Seseorang yang tidak dikenal dan berlemak itu menggedor-gedor pintunya dengan keras dan memaki-makinya dengan bahasa yang tidak pernah ia dengar. Namun ia tidak menghiraukannya dan berharap hari berlalu begitu saja. Hingga tetangga lain harus mengambil peran mengusir seseorang yang asing itu, hingga tak pernah lagi terlihat batang hidungnya. Gadis itu mendapat satu hal yang ia percaya sampai sekarang. Jangan pernah percaya seorangpun yang berjanji menghapus angka. Pondasi yang ia percaya lebih kuat dibandingkan memori seberharga apapun.

Namun sekarang sedikit berbeda. Sangat meyakinkan, dan sang gadis terpikat oleh tampak dan ucapan perempuan itu. Ia merasa yang ia dapatkan tidak cuma-cuma — ia bekerja kepadanya, menjaga nyala yang tak begitu ia paham apa maksudnya. Itu pertukaran yang wajar, lalu ia mengangguk pelan dan segera mengemas keperluannya. Sekiranya hal hal yang diperlukan untuk *pekerjaan* barunya. Tapi ia teringat akan sesuatu, dan berlari kecil ke arah pintu.
“Beri aku beberapa waktu, rajutan ini harus kuselesaikan. Pembelinya memercayakan angkanya padaku” kata gadis itu lirih, namun dengan nafas sedikit tersengal
Perempuan itu tampak menimbang sesuatu dalam benaknya, cukup lama hingga membuat suasana sedikit menghangat dan nafas gadis itu kembali normal.

“Baiklah” Balas perempuan bertopi itu dengan nada antusias. “Selesaikan, dan aku akan menjemputmu besok pagi” lanjutnya lalu ia berbalik dan sedikit mendadahi gadis itu. Langkahnya begitu anggun, saking anggunnya serasa ia melayang diatas tanah. Sekilas gadis itu merasa bahwa cuaca semakin mendingin dan ia kembali masuk kedalam rumah. Berharap rajutannya selesai dalam semalam.

Dan pagi akhirnya menyingsing di ufuk timur. Ia terbangun di antara lilitan wol dan rajutan sweater yang semalam ia garap. Benang-benang kusut menggantung di jemarinya seperti sisa mimpi yang belum selesai. Gadis itu sulit sekali tidur awalnya; utang-utang itu adalah angka yang memenuhi pikirannya malam itu. Dan juga perempuan asing yang menawarkan menghapus angka dengan sebuah nyala, sesuatu yang bahkan sulit ia bayangkan bentuknya.
Namun sebelum tertidur, gadis itu sempat berharap sedikit saja — untuk percaya pada sesuatu selain ibu dan angka-angka. Dan karena harapan kecil itulah, ia akhirnya tertidur tanpa mimpi buruk.
Anehnya, pagi itu terasa hangat. Bukan hangat musim semi yang biasa menyelinap malu-malu dari sela jendela. Hangat ini diam. Menempel di kulit seperti napas seseorang yang berdiri terlalu dekat.

Gadis itu membuka matanya perlahan. Tak ada embun di kaca jendela. Tak ada uap tipis keluar dari mulutnya. Ia terdiam cukup lama memandangi kedua telapak tangannya sendiri. Diputar perlahan seolah memastikan itu memang miliknya. Lalu tanpa sadar ia meraih sisi ranjang yang biasanya kosong dan dingin. Tetapi pagi itu bahkan ruang kosong terasa hangat.
Seketika tubuh gadis itu menegang.

Rumah tua itu biasanya berderit saat pagi tiba. Kayu-kayunya selalu berbunyi kecil seperti orang tua yang mengeluh pelan. Namun pagi ini rumah itu terlalu sunyi. Terlalu diam. Seolah sesuatu sedang mendengarkan. Lalu dari lantai bawah, terdengar ketukan lembut dari arah pintu depan. Suara ketokan itu terdengar pelan, seperti ketukan kuku pada kayu basah. Dan gadis itu yakin, perempuan itu hadir tepat sesuai dengan ia janjikan.

Dengan gelagapan gadis itu menarik dirinya dari kasur, dan memperbaiki pakaiannya. Ia membuka jendela yang menghembuskan kehangatan yang ganjil, ia melihat ke arah bawah dan menyadari perempuan itu sudah dari awal menghadap keatas dengan senyum lembut, mata yang sendu, dan ayunan lengan yang anggun seolah mendadahi. Gadis itu mengangguk diam lalu menutup kembali jendelanya dengan pelan.
Pintu kayu itu terbuka, memperlihatkan sang gadis yang berdiri kaku dengan tas tentengan berat di tangannya.
"Hai, sayang. Kau sudah siap?" sapa perempuan itu sekejap. Senyumnya kini semakin lebar, merentang di wajahnya dengan cara yang terkesan dipaksakan.

“Aku siap, tapi izinkan aku mengantarkan rajutan ini kepada tetanggaku” balas gadis itu tergesa, meski tanpa balasan dari perempuan itu. Sang gadis tetap berbelok ke arah kanan melewati beberapa rumah-rumah monoton disebelahnya. Tapi perempuan itu tetap diam dan mengikutinya pelan tanpa suara dari belakang.

Langkah kaki sang gadis terdengar berderit memecah keheningan pagi, beradu dengan tanah berembun yang mulai mengeras. Namun, betapapun tajam ia menajamkan telinga, tak ada satu pun bunyi langkah yang mengikutinya. Perempuan bertopi itu bergerak seperti bayangan—mengambang, menyapu jalanan tanpa meninggalkan jejak, membawa serta hawa hangat yang secara ganjil membuat bulu kuduk sang gadis meremang.

Setibanya di depan pintu kayu bernoda kusam milik tetangganya, gadis itu mengetuk pelan. Pintu berderit terbuka, menampilkan wajah keriput sang tetangga yang tampak memikul lelah dari sisa malam. Namun, raut kelelahan itu lenyap seketika, tergantikan oleh pupil mata yang membesar dan napas yang mendadak tertahan. Tatapan wanita tua itu tidak tertuju pada sang gadis, melainkan terkunci lurus menembus bahunya.
"Rajutannya sudah selesai, Nyonya. Sesuai janjiku," kata gadis itu, memecah kecanggungan, seraya menyodorkan lipatan wol yang rapi.

Sang tetangga tidak segera merespons. Tangannya yang tiba-tiba gemetar perlahan meraih rajutan itu, sementara matanya masih melebar menatap sosok anggun di belakang sang gadis. Udara di beranda itu perlahan terasa sumpek, seolah oksigen perlahan diisap habis dari sekeliling mereka. Dengan gerakan kaku dan sangat tergesa, sang tetangga menyelipkan beberapa keping koin ke telapak tangan gadis itu yang dingin.

"Ambil ini," bisik tetangga itu, suaranya parau dan nyaris terdengar seperti rintihan. Jemarinya mencengkeram pergelangan tangan sang gadis sejenak dengan kuat. "Dan pergilah... jangan pernah melihat ke belakang saat kau berjalan."
Pintu dibanting tertutup seketika. Terdengar bunyi rentetan palang besi ditarik dari dalam, seolah mengunci sebuah teror agar tak bisa masuk ke rumahnya.

Gadis itu mematung, menatap kepingan koin di tangannya—angka-angka terakhir yang ia terima, yang entah mengapa kini terasa sama sekali tidak ada harganya. Ia menelan ludah, teringat peringatan tetangganya, namun instingnya memaksanya menoleh perlahan.

Perempuan bertopi itu masih di sana. Hanya saja, jaraknya kini jauh lebih dekat dari sebelumnya, berdiri tepat di hadapannya hingga sang gadis bisa mencium aroma manis yang memualkan. Senyum paksaan itu masih menempel sempurna di wajahnya, tak bergeser satu milimeter pun sejak ia berada di depan rumah.
"Sudah selesai mengucapkan selamat tinggal pada angka-angkamu, sayang?" tanyanya lembut.
Anehnya, bibir perempuan itu sama sekali tidak bergerak. Suara yang selimut itu kini tidak lagi mengalun di udara, melainkan menggema langsung, berat dan menyesakkan, di dalam kepala sang gadis.
Dengan gadis itu kini sepenuhnya menyadari bahwa ia berhadapan dengan sesuatu yang jauh di luar nalar manusia, ke arah mana perempuan bertopi itu akan menuntunnya berjalan sekarang?

Tak pernah rasanya gadis itu berjalan sejauh ini. Seumur hidupnya, peta dunianya hanyalah jalan menuju pasar, ladang-ladang mati, dan sungai yang membeku. Kini tubuh mungilnya dipaksa menyeret tas yang terasa semakin berat, berbanding terbalik dengan perempuan di depannya. Sosok itu melangkah tanpa bersusah payah, pakaiannya yang berat dan berlapis tampak... berkibar, seolah ia memiliki anginnya sendiri.

Sesekali perempuan itu bersenandung. Nada ganjil yang tak pernah gadis itu dengar sebelumnya. Ia juga mulai berceloteh betapa sulitnya menemukan gadis sepertinya—dan yang membuat perut sang gadis kembali mual, suara celotehan serasa masih menggema pelan di dalam kepalanya, sementara dilihat dari belakang, bahu dan postur perempuan itu diam tak bergerak.
“Aku yakin kamu pernah bertemu pria gemuk sebelumnya” katanya lirih yang sekali lagi menggema di telinga sang gadis.

Langkah gadis itu tertahan. Sepatunya bergesekan pelan dengan tanah beku. Perutnya bergejolak, membangkitkan kembali memori tentang napas panas yang berat dan tatapan dari pria berlemak tempo hari. Ketakutan merayap perlahan naik ke tengkuknya.
Perempuan itu ikut berhenti, meski punggungnya tetap membelakangi sang gadis. Angin seketika mati, menyisakan keheningan yang menekan dada.

"Tatapannya kotor dan lapar, bukan?" suara itu kembali mengalir pelan di dalam tempurung kepala sang gadis, halus namun terasa menguliti. "Menatapmu seolah kau adalah sepotong daging segar yang tak berdaya... atau mungkin, sebuah wadah kosong yang bebas ia isi dengan kebusukannya. Entah dia sekadar pria malang yang dikendalikan oleh berahi liarnya, atau sesuatu yang jauh lebih purba dan lebih lapar dari itu... niatnya selalu sama rendahnya."

Gadis itu mencengkeram erat tali tasnya hingga buku-buku jarinya memutih. Udara dingin yang biasa ia temani kini terasa meremang. Ia mulai menyadari bahwa selama ini dirinya tidak hanya sedang miskin, tetapi juga sedang diintai; dipelajari layaknya buruan yang tersesat.

"Namun, wajar saja banyak yang mengincarmu, sayang," gema suara itu melanjutkan, kini nadanya melembut, menyerupai simpati palsu dari seseorang yang sedang mengagumi porselen rapuh. "Kau memancarkan keputusasaan yang begitu murni. Gadis belia dengan tangan yang selalu membeku, bersikeras melindungi memori yang perlahan retak. Sesuatu yang sangat menggugah selera untuk direnggut."

Gadis itu menelan ludah yang terasa tajam di tenggorokannya. Instingnya berteriak untuk menjatuhkan tasnya dan berlari kembali ke desa, tetapi kakinya seolah telah berakar pada tanah yang hangat di bawah pijakannya.

"Tapi dia terlalu bising. Terlalu vulgar," tawa kecil menyusul, memantul di dalam kepala gadis itu tanpa menggetarkan bahu si perempuan bertopi sama sekali. "Aku tahu kau tidak naif. Kau memiliki batas tentang keputusasaan mana yang sudi kau terima. Itulah mengapa aku tidak repot-repot mengusir makhluk berlemak itu hari itu. Karena sejak awal... aku sangat meyakini, pada akhirnya kau akan tetap ikut bersamaku."

Perempuan itu akhirnya berbalik perlahan. Bayangan dari pinggiran topinya menutupi separuh wajahnya, menyisakan senyum melengkung yang kini terlihat menegang dan terlampau lebar—menunggu sang gadis melangkah maju memecah kesunyian yang mencekam.

Tanpa mengatakan apa-apa lagi, perempuan itu mengangkat satu tangannya yang terbalut sarung tangan rajut, menunjuk ke arah depan. Gadis itu menelan ludah yang terasa tajam di tenggorokannya, lalu memberanikan diri mengikuti arah telunjuk tersebut.
Matanya perlahan melebar, napasnya seolah ditarik paksa dari paru-parunya.

Kabut tebal yang sejak tadi mengaburkan pandangan mereka perlahan menyibak mundur, seolah ketakutan pada eksistensi jari perempuan itu. Di hadapan mereka, bumi tidak lagi mendatar. Peta dunia yang selama ini gadis itu kenal telah terputus di ujung jalan ini. Tanah di depannya terbelah membentuk sebuah jurang atau lubang raksasa yang melingkar sempurna—seolah dunia pernah berlubang karena ada sesuatu yang raksasa baru saja dicabut dari sana.

Dan di dasar jurang yang sangat dalam itu, tidak ada salju. Tidak ada es yang membeku. Hanya ada sebuah struktur bangunan megah yang menjulang dari kayu hitam legam, terdistorsi seperti rumah panggung yang dibangun terbalik. Rumah itu berdiri sunyi di tengah lautan kabut hangat yang berdenyut pelan, menanti penghuni barunya.

"Kau ingat aku berjanji tentang kamar di dasar rumahku?" bisik perempuan itu. Kali ini suaranya benar-benar keluar dari celah bibirnya sendiri, memecah keheningan absolut di tepi jurang itu. "Mari kita turun menemui nyalamu."

Maka gadis itu ikut menuruni tangga ke dasar rumah, begitu panjang dan terasa tanpa ujung. Gadis itu semakin terseok-seok semakin kelelahan ketika di harus menuruni tangga dengan membawa tas yang berat. Perempuan itu sedikit melirik ke kanan dan bergumam dengan bahasa yang masih gadis itu belum pahami. Dalam sekejap bawaannya terasa ringan, seolah dia tidak membawa apapun. Gadis masih tidak percaya lalu memeriksa isi dari bawaanya. Yang ternyata masih utuh tidak berkurang satu apapun, anehnya dia tidak lagi terkejut dengan keanehan di hadapannya. Jauh di lubuk hatinya dia percaya, yang bersamanya bukanlah manusia.

Tangga batu itu merentang terlalu panjang. Jauh lebih panjang dari kedalaman yang bisa dijangkau nalar manusia, menukik turun menembus kabut hingga ia mulai meragukan apakah jurang ini benar-benar memiliki dasar.
“Sampai kapan tangga ini selesai?” tanya gadis itu dengan nada yang polos dan tersengal-sengal.
“Sampai kau siap sayangg…. oh sampai kau siap” jawab perempuan itu sedikit tertawa.
Waktu luruh dan membusuk di atas anak tangga itu. Gadis itu tidak tahu apakah mereka telah turun selama berjam-jam, berhari-hari, atau hanya dalam tarikan satu napas yang panjang.

Pada awalnya, kebiasaan lama gadis itu mengambil alih. Dalam diam ia mulai menghitung anak tangga di dalam kepalanya. *Seratus satu, seratus dua, seribu lima ratus, entah keberapa ribu.* Mengakar pada nalurinya yang selalu dihadapkan pada hutang dan hari-hari yang bisa diukur. Setiap kali ia menambahkan satu angka baru, kabut hangat di bawah mereka terasa semakin tebal, dan dasar jurang itu seolah terus menjauh, mengejek usahanya.

Di depannya, perempuan bertopi itu terus melangkah tanpa suara, sesekali bersenandung dengan nada yang kini terdengar seperti lolongan angin yang dihaluskan. Setiap ketukan dari senandung itu seolah melolosi satu angka dari kepala sang gadis. Semakin gadis itu mencoba mengingat jumlah hutang ibunya, tagihan para tabib, atau sisa koin di tangannya—semuanya perlahan kabur. Menjadi abu.
Lalu, sebuah kesadaran menghantam dada sang gadis, sedingin es namun sejelas kristal.
*“Sampai kau siap...”*

Kata-kata itu kembali terngiang. Selama ia masih menghitung anak tangga, selama ia masih menjadikan angka sebagai jangkar rasionalitasnya, tangga ini tidak akan pernah menyentuh dasar. Dunia ini bukan dunia yang bisa diukur. Ini adalah dunia tempat memori dan emosi menjadi mata uang tunggal.

Maka, pada satu tarikan napas yang panjang dan gemetar, sang gadis berhenti menghitung. Ia memaksa kepalanya membuang sisa-sisa koin, menenggelamkan deretan hutang ibunya, dan hanya memegang satu hal: memori tentang hembusan napas hangat ibunya di tangannya setiap pagi. Ia tidak peduli lagi pada anak tangga keberapa ia berpijak. Ia hanya berjalan, tenggelam dalam ingatan yang murni.
Tepat ketika angka terakhir pudar dari benaknya, ujung sepatunya membentur sesuatu yang padat dan berbunyi tumpul. Bukan lagi papan kayu, melainkan ubin batu hitam yang mengkilap oleh embun.
Gadis itu membuka matanya lebar-lebar. Tangga itu telah berakhir.

Mereka berdiri di dasar jurang. Struktur rumah panggung yang terbalik itu kini menjulang tepat di hadapannya, menekan langit-langit kabut dengan auranya yang pekat dan absolut. Ujung atapnya menancap ke dalam bumi, sementara fondasinya—yang seharusnya berada di tanah—justru mencengkeram kekosongan di atas sana. Di bagian paling bawah rumah aneh itu, terdapat sebuah pintu kayu ek berukir yang tampak sudah berabad-abad usianya.

Perempuan bertopi itu melangkah ke samping, tidak lagi menghalangi jalan. Gadis itu menoleh dan menyadari sebuah perubahan yang mengerikan. Senyum paksaan yang sejak tadi merentang di wajah perempuan itu kini telah raib sepenuhnya. Wajahnya kosong, tak berekspresi, tak bernyawa. Sorot matanya yang sendu kini hanyalah dua lubang gelap yang menatap lurus menembus jiwa sang gadis, seolah esensi yang tadi berpura-pura menjadi manusia kini telah kembali ke wujud aslinya yang apatis.

Pintu kayu ek itu terbuka perlahan tanpa suara, menghembuskan udara yang berbau seperti buku tua, kemenyan, dan sesuatu yang manis namun hangus. Di dalam kegelapan pekat ruangan itu, berjarak beberapa belas langkah ke dalam, ada seberkas cahaya keemasan yang berdenyut lemah. Terang dan redup. Terang dan redup. Bernapas.

"Masuklah," suara perempuan itu kini terdengar seperti beribu-ribu daun kering yang bergesekan, tak lagi menggema di kepala sang gadis, melainkan berbisik tepat di telinganya. "Nyalamu menunggumu. Temani dia. Dan ingat..."
Perempuan itu sedikit membungkuk, wajah datarnya kini hanya berjarak satu jengkal dari wajah sang gadis.
"...jangan biarkan dia tertidur."

Dan dengan langkah yang gemetar, sang gadis memasuki ruangan tersebut. Di balik pintu ruangan tanpa jendela, tanpa suara, tanpa apa-apa selain sebuah nyala kecil di atas dudukan kecil di tengah ruangan.
"Mengapa begitu sunyi?" tanya gadis itu, sebab di kamar itu ia bisa mendengar darahnya sendiri berjalan, sebuah desir lembut seperti seseorang bersenandung di kejauhan.

"Supaya nyala itu tidak terganggu," kata perempuan bertopi. "Dan supaya kau tidak pernah merasa sendiri. Dengar — rumah berbisik kepadamu, agar kau punya teman." Ia menunjuk nyala itu. "Selama kau menyayanginya, ia akan menyala. Setiap kali kau menyayanginya, sedikit kehangatanmu berpindah kepadanya. Begitulah cinta, sayang. Cinta selalu begitu."

Lalu perempuan itu melangkah keluar. Pintu kayu tertutup tanpa bunyi. Sang gadis kini duduk sendirian di samping nyala kecilnya, menatap pendar yang berdenyut redup. Dan untuk pertama kalinya sejak ibunya tidak lagi bangun—jauh di kedalaman simpang siur kebingungan dan ketakutannya—gadis itu merasa berguna.
Musim dingin pertama datang dengan lembut.

Gadis itu tidak melihatnya datang — tidak ada jendela — tapi ia merasakannya dari nyala itu, yang meredup sedikit, seujung kuku, seolah mengantuk. *Tidurlah, nyala kecil*, gadis itu hampir berkata, lalu teringat bahwa justru itu yang tak boleh terjadi. Maka ia membalik kalimat ibunya. *"Jangan tidur, nyala kecil,"* bisiknya. *"Biar aku yang berjaga."* Dan ia mencondongkan tubuhnya, menyayangi nyala itu sekuat yang ia bisa, dan nyala itu pun terang kembali.

Pagi itu—gadis itu menyebutnya pagi, walau tak ada pagi di dasar rumah—ia hanya merasa bahwa tepat setelah ia bangun dari tidur, itu adalah pagi. Tangannya lebih dingin dari biasanya. Tapi ia tidak keberatan. Ia sudah biasa berteman dengan dingin. Dan bukankah perempuan bertopi berkata ia tidak akan pernah dingin lagi? Tentu maksudnya nanti. Tentu kehangatan itu akan datang nanti, setelah ia membuktikan dirinya, seperti segala hal baik selalu datang nanti.

Anehnya, tubuhnya seolah mengerti bahwa ia kini berada di dunia yang tidak lagi membutuhkan hal-hal biasa. Berhari-hari atau mungkin berminggu-minggu berlalu—ia tak tahu pasti—perutnya tidak pernah merengek meminta diisi. Tenggorokannya tak lagi menagih air. Bahkan rasa ingin membuang hajat pun menguap begitu saja. Di dalam kamar tanpa jendela itu, ia tidak lagi merasa seperti manusia seutuhnya; ia seolah perlahan berubah menjadi seonggok perasaan yang hanya diberi tugas untuk duduk, bernapas, dan menjaga.

Satu-satunya hal manusiawi yang sesekali datang menyapanya hanyalah rasa kantuk yang teramat berat. Awalnya, gadis itu ketakutan. Ia meremas jemarinya kuat-kuat, menggigit bibirnya, dan terus melotot menatap nyala itu. *Biar aku yang berjaga*, bisiknya pada diri sendiri, takut jika ia terlelap sebentar saja, nyala itu akan ikut mati. Namun, kesunyian kamar itu terlalu tebal dan membelai kepalanya seperti lagu pengantar tidur yang tak bisa dilawan. Pada akhirnya, ia selalu menyerah. Tubuhnya merosot ke lantai dingin, dan ia terlelap tanpa mimpi.

Lalu setiap kali ia terbangun dari lelapnya yang panjang, selalu ada sesuatu yang berubah di sudut ruangan. Benda-benda muncul dalam diam seolah kamar itu melahirkannya saat ia menutup mata. Kadang secangkir air putih atau sepotong biskuit keras yang anehnya cukup membuat perutnya terasa penuh berhari-hari. Namun yang paling sering muncul adalah tumpukan buku tua bersampul kusam.

Gadis itu tak punya hal lain untuk dilakukan, maka ia membaca. Buku-buku itu berisi kisah-kisah aneh dari tempat yang tak ia kenal, namun perasaan sepinya terasa begitu dekat. Ia membaca tentang seorang anak perempuan yang terus mengayun sendirian di taman bermain yang mati, menunggu sosok yang dikira teman padahal monster. Di lembaran lain, ia menemukan kisah tentang sebuah toko bunga muram tempat seseorang merangkai duka di atas kertas. Dan ada juga cerita yang membuatnya termenung lama; tentang seorang pria yang putus asa menggali makam kosong di dekat sekumpulan bunga biru, mencari-cari istrinya yang hilang.

Bahkan di salah satu halaman yang sedikit robek, ia menemukan deskripsi tentang makhluk bergelambir lemak yang mengembara memangsa keputusasaan manusia—membuat gadis itu bergidik pelan, teringat pada napas berat di balik pintunya dulu.

Selain itu kadang kadang buku-buku itu berisi kisah-kisah atau mungkin sejarah dari dunia yang tak pernah ia ketahui. Ada tulisan tentang makhluk-makhluk tak bermata yang memakan gema suara, tentang peradaban yang dibangun di atas kelopak mata raksasa yang tertidur, dan tentang ritual-ritual kuno di mana bayangan manusia bisa dikuliti. Membaca buku-buku aneh itu menjadi rutinitas barunya, mengalihkan pikirannya dari kesunyian absolut yang menekan dinding-dinding batu. Cerita-cerita kelam di dalam lembaran berdebu itu entah mengapa terasa memvalidasi kesedihannya, seolah berbisik kepadanya bahwa dunia di atas sana memang terlalu rusak untuk ditinggali.

Dan setiap selesai membaca, ia akan kembali pada rutinitasnya. Mencondongkan tubuh, menyayangi nyala di depannya hingga terang kembali, lalu merapatkan tangan dan mulai menghitung untuk memastikan dirinya masih ada.

Ia menghitung, untuk menemani diri. Ia menghitung bukan jam, karena tak ada jam, melainkan berapa banyak hal yang masih ia ingat dari atas sana. Wajah ibunya. Bau hujan di tanah. Rasa garam. Nama sungai di dekat rumahnya. Ia menyimpannya seperti orang menyimpan bintang, dan berkata pada dirinya: selama aku masih bisa menghitungnya, aku masih aku.
Musim dingin ke 3 datang tanpa pemberitahuan.

Kali ini nyala itu tidak meredup seujung kuku, melainkan hampir separuh, dan gadis itu harus mencondong lebih dekat, harus menyayangi lebih keras, harus memberi lebih banyak. Ia memberi nyala itu nama sungai di dekat rumahnya, karena ia pikir mungkin nyala itu akan suka punya nama. Ketika nyala itu terang kembali, gadis itu sadar ia tidak bisa lagi mengingat nama sungai itu. Ia telah memberikannya. Itu yang dimaksud memberi.
Tidak apa-apa, katanya pada diri sendiri. *Aku masih ingat wajah Ibu. Aku masih ingat bau hujan. Aku masih punya bintang-bintangku. Aku masih ingat banyak hal.*

Namun jauh di bilik hatinya, ada rasa rindu yang berdenyut akan dunia luar. Dan entah sampai kapan ia harus terus menyayangi sesuatu yang bahkan ia tak pernah tahu wujud aslinya. Sesuatu yang ganjil, sesuatu yang mengerikan.
*Tapi anehnya, aku semakin menyayanginya,* batin sang gadis, menatap pendar keemasan itu dengan mata yang perlahan meredup. *Dan aku tak rela meninggalkannya.*
Tiba-tiba, entah dalam sekian lama. Pintu terbuka sekali, di musim dingin ketiga itu. Bukan perempuan bertopi, melainkan suaranya saja, turun dari atas tangga yang panjang.
"Kau menjaganya dengan baik, sayang," kata suara itu.
"Berapa lama lagi?" tanya gadis itu. Suaranya terdengar asing, terlalu nyaring di kamar yang memakan suara.

Hening sebentar. Hening yang terlalu panjang untuk pertanyaan sesederhana itu. "Sampai ada yang menggantikanmu," kata suara itu, lembut sekali, selembut selimut. "Begitulah caranya. Ibumu dulu juga menjaga sebuah nyala, tahukah kau? Setiap penjaga boleh naik, boleh pulang, boleh beristirahat — tapi hanya setelah ia menemukan seseorang yang tangannya cukup dingin, dan hatinya cukup penyayang, untuk turun menggantikannya."

Gadis itu terdiam. Ibunya yang setiap pagi menghangatkan tangannya dengan napas. Ibunya yang tangannya, kalau gadis itu jujur pada dirinya sendiri, selalu lebih dingin daripada tangan siapa pun yang pernah ia sentuh.
"Bagaimana caranya," tanya gadis itu pelan, "menemukan orang itu?"

"Kau ceritakan kepadanya sebuah dongeng," kata suara itu. "Dongeng yang indah, tentang nyala kecil yang harus dijaga, dan kehangatan yang menanti, dan ibu yang tidak pernah pergi. Ceritakan dengan lembut. Mereka selalu percaya, asal kau ceritakan dengan lembut."

Lalu pintu tertutup, dan gadis itu sendiri lagi dengan nyalanya, dan untuk pertama kalinya ia memperhatikan sesuatu yang seharusnya ia perhatikan sejak lama: bahwa nyala kecil itu, kalau ia mendekatkan wajahnya cukup dekat, tidaklah seperti api.
Ia berdetak.
Musim dingin yang tidak pernah berakhir.

Gadis itu — meski sekarang sukar menyebutnya gadis, karena waktu di dasar rumah tidak menuakan tubuh melainkan mengikis sesuatu yang lebih dalam — ia telah memberikan kepada nyala itu bau hujan, rasa garam, dan segala hal yang ia ingat. Sampai akhirnya, pada suatu musim dingin yang panjangnya tak bisa ia hitung lagi, wajah ibunya. Ia memberikannya karena nyala itu hampir padam dan tak ada lagi yang tersisa untuk diberikan, dan ketika nyala itu terang kembali ia mencoba mengingat siapa yang barusan ia korbankan, dan tidak bisa.
Ia mendekatkan wajahnya ke nyala itu, sedekat yang ia bisa. Dan di dalam nyala kecil yang berdetak itu, ia melihat sebuah wajah.

Wajahnya sendiri. Muda, dengan tangan yang masih bisa merasakan dingin, di hari ketika seorang perempuan bertopi mengetuk pintunya dan berkata *aku dengar kau pandai menemani yang dingin.* Nyala itu bukan sesuatu yang ia jaga. Nyala itu adalah dirinya — bara terakhir dari seorang gadis yang sedang padam, sangat pelan, lebih pelan daripada yang dimaksudkan alam mana pun, karena ada satu kesadaran yang menempel padanya dan menolak, karena cinta, karena selalu karena cinta, melepaskannya.

Tidak ada nyala lain. Tidak ada nyala lain yang pernah ia jaga selain nyawanya sendiri, yang dijaganya tetap menyala bukan demi hidup melainkan demi *menjaga* — sebuah tugas yang memakan persis benda yang ia gunakan untuk menjaganya. Setiap kali ia menyayanginya, sedikit kehangatannya berpindah. Begitulah cinta. Cinta selalu begitu.

Dan ibunya — yang tangannya selalu dingin, yang setiap pagi memberinya napas, yang pada suatu pagi tidak bangun — ibunya tidak pernah pergi. Ibunya hanya berhasil. Ibunya hanya menemukan seseorang yang tangannya cukup dingin dan hatinya cukup penyayang, dan menceritainya sebuah dongeng dengan lembut, dan naik ke atas tangga yang panjang, dan beristirahat akhirnya, akhirnya, setelah entah berapa musim dingin yang tak terhitung.
*Tidurlah, nyala kecil, biar Ibu yang berjaga.*
Tidak ada Ibu. "Ibu" adalah nama yang diberikan kepada siapa pun yang sedang menjaga nyala. Suatu hari nama itu akan jadi namanya. Dan ia tenggelam

Ia tak lagi ingat siapa dirinya, siapa wajah di balik pendaran cahaya itu, atau apa sebenarnya tugas yang mengikatnya di sana. Segalanya telah tuntas ia serahkan hanya agar nyala itu tetap bernapas. Kini, ia sekadar duduk mematung. Sepasang matanya menatap kosong, tak berkedip untuk satu kali pun, tak mengenali apa pun. Gunung buku yang menumpuk entah ribuan atau jutaan di sudut ruangan kini hanyalah lanskap bisu baginya. Boro-boro mengingat isinya; untuk sekadar mengeja dan membaca pun... ia tak lagi tahu caranya.

Tiba-tiba, pintu kayu ek itu berdecit memecah keheningan yang telah menggenang entah berapa eon lamanya. Perempuan bertopi itu kembali hadir. Senyum paksaannya telah tanggal, menyisakan sepasang mata yang sendu dan penuh duka.
“Akhirnya kau tak punya apa-apa lagi, sayang... maafkan aku,” bisiknya parau. “Tapi itulah tugasmu.”

Perempuan itu berjongkok, mengulurkan tangannya, dan mengusap lembut rambut sang gadis yang diam membisu. Sang gadis telah melupakan perempuan di hadapannya. Ia telah melupakan segalanya. Namun, tepat di bawah usapan tangan itu, sebersit rindu purba dan kehangatan yang asing mendadak merayap di dadanya.
Dan tanpa ia tahu apa itu kesedihan, tanpa ia ingat bagaimana caranya berduka, sebulir air mata jatuh melewati pipinya yang membeku.

“Aku kembalikan kamu ke atas. Kuberikan kamu tugas terakhir, jalani hidupmu dengan baik mulai saat ini. Beristirahatlah, dan akan kudongengkan kisah terakhir agar kau selalu ingat” Kata perempuan itu sekali lagi, dan begitulah sang gadis tertidur dengan dongengan terakhir sang perempuan bertopi.
Maka begini, anakku. Begini akhir dongengnya, dan dengarkan baik-baik, sebab ini bagian yang penting.

Pada suatu masa hiduplah seorang gadis yang tangannya selalu dingin, dan ia diberi sebuah tugas yang indah: menjaga sebuah nyala kecil agar musim semi tetap tinggal di rumah. Dan ia menjaganya dengan setia, dengan sepenuh cinta, selama bertahun-tahun yang lebih panjang daripada yang bisa kauhitung — sampai pada suatu hari pintu di atas tangga terbuka, dan turunlah seorang anak dengan tangan yang dingin, dan hati yang penyayang, dan utang-utang yang ingin sekali ia hapuskan.
Lihat tanganmu, sayang. Begitu dingin. Kemarilah, duduk di sampingku, dekat dengan nyala kecil ini.
Dengar bagaimana ia berdetak.
Biar kuceritakan betapa hangatnya nanti.

en.title: At the Bottom of the House
en.excerpt: Once upon a time, in the heart of a beautiful hinterland village, the seasons always arrived gently. The spring sowed beauty, while the summer heat offered shade—only occasionally coaxing…
body: Once upon a time, in the heart of a beautiful hinterland village, the seasons always arrived gently. The spring sowed beauty, while the summer heat offered shade—only occasionally coaxing beads of sweat to fall shyly from the villagers' faces. The cold, too, was calming, giving the people a brief respite to enjoy the fruits of their hard work. Back then, the seasons were reluctant to trouble the villagers, arriving slowly, whistling through small lightning at the edge of the night to signal the coming change. Right beneath it lived a sweet girl full of warmth, despite her hands always being cold. Gazing hopefully, praying perhaps, that her life would be filled with beautiful memories.

However, those friendly seasons seemed to halt before the door of a large house now slowly decaying. Inside, the young girl had to count numbers that troubled her quite a bit—for her, it was a lot, far too much, so much that she recounted them on paper three times just to be sure she wasn't misreading the number of zeroes. For a moment, the girl let out a long sigh while rubbing her hands together; it was a piercingly cold winter. Her sigh even formed a thin puff of steam. *Strange,* she thought, *winter doesn't usually play this cruelly.*

Her thoughts seemed to echo in the house that was far too large to heat, making the atmosphere even more piercing. The sheer size of this house no longer guaranteed prosperity, because they were now too poor to repair it. And since childhood, she had learned that the cold wasn't something to be fought, but something to be befriended, like a sickly younger sibling whom you could never hate even when they exhausted you.

Then, the girl furrowed her brow slightly while twirling the ends of her brownish-black hair. The cold air bit into the reddish skin of her face, and instantly she rubbed her cheeks with both hands, muttering softly.
"Why does the world offer me a world that can be measured? Instead of a world that can be remembered."

Then, the girl fell back into contemplation. Twirling a pen that was almost out of ink because she constantly wore it down calculating numbers. To her, the world was nothing more than numbers, and she was disappointed by that fact. No, not because she felt burdened by all these numbers. But she was terrified that her beautiful memories would be replaced by the numbers popping up one by one.

The bills from the healers inside and outside the village were numbers. The remaining debts for household needs were numbers. The days Mother had left, according to almost all the healers, somehow felt like numbers—though no one dared write them down explicitly.

Even though all these things weighed on the girl's mind, there was one thing she remembered. Her mother warmed the girl's hands with her breath every morning, and every morning said the exact same thing: *Sleep, little flame, let Mother keep watch.* And the girl would smile in a half-awake state, celebrating the dreams she had just dreamt. The two of them would laugh, and the girl would go back to sleep with a small smile.

Then, one morning, her mother didn't wake up again. The clock on the wall kept ticking, but no one was breathing in that room anymore. And no one warmed the girl's hands anymore, and the large house became as cold as she had always feared. Not only was she now entirely alone, but that memory, in whatever number it was, would also disappear. The girl thought about that constantly, always.

So, when dusk was almost breaking and a woman in a hat came knocking—a woman whose face was as soothing as the afternoon, whose voice was like a blanket—the girl opened the door slowly; she had just been knitting a neighbor's clothes, for a wage, of course.
"I hear," the woman said, "you are good at keeping the cold company."
"I am not good at anything," the girl replied coldly.

"That is exactly the skill I mean," the woman said, and smiled. "I have a job for you, dear. A warm job. At the bottom of my house, there is a room, and in that room, there is a small flame, and that flame must not go out. Your only task is to guard it. Sit beside it, and love it, and do not let it sleep. In exchange, you will never be cold again, and your mother"—the woman touched the girl's cheek, and her hand was warm, incredibly warm—"your mother will be at peace where she is, because the debts she left behind will be erased, as if they never existed."

The girl fell silent for a moment. Thinking about all the trouble those numbers had caused. She remembered someone once promising the exact same thing, but that person had terrible breath and an unpleasant face. Flabs of fat hanging under his chin, on his arms, on his belly, and in every place one might not even think of; she was certain that person was a man of fat. The girl didn't understand why anyone would willingly trouble themselves to pay off numbers that even she found troublesome. But when she saw, once again, the heavy breathing of that fat person panting and perhaps... hot. She decided against accepting the offer and slammed her door shut.

That unknown, fat person pounded on her door violently and cursed her in a language she had never heard. But she ignored him and hoped the day would simply pass. Until other neighbors had to step in to chase the stranger away, until he was never seen again. The girl gained one thing she believed to this day: *Never trust anyone who promises to erase numbers.* The foundation she believed in was stronger than any memory, no matter how precious.

But now, it was slightly different. Very convincing, and the girl was captivated by the woman's appearance and words. She felt that what she was getting wasn't for free—she was working for her, guarding a flame whose purpose she didn't quite understand. It was a fair exchange, so she nodded slowly and immediately packed her necessities. Just the things needed for her new job. But she remembered something, and jogged toward the door.
"Give me some time; I have to finish this knitting. The buyer entrusted their numbers to me," the girl said softly, though slightly out of breath.
The woman seemed to weigh something in her mind, long enough that the atmosphere warmed slightly and the girl's breathing returned to normal.

"Alright," the woman in the hat replied enthusiastically. "Finish it, and I will pick you up tomorrow morning," she continued, then turned and waved slightly at the girl. Her steps were so graceful, so graceful it felt as if she were hovering above the ground. For a fleeting moment, the girl felt the weather growing colder, and she went back inside the house. Hoping the knitting would be finished overnight.

And morning finally broke on the eastern horizon. She woke up amidst tangles of yarn and the sweater she had worked on last night. Tangled threads hung from her fingers like the remnants of an unfinished dream. The girl had a very hard time falling asleep at first; those debts were numbers filling her mind that night. And also the strange woman who offered to erase the numbers with a flame, something she could barely even picture.

But before falling asleep, the girl had allowed herself to hope just a little—to believe in something other than her mother and numbers. And because of that small hope, she finally slept without nightmares.

Strangely, that morning felt warm. Not the spring warmth that usually sneaked in shyly through the window cracks. This warmth was silent. Clinging to the skin like the breath of someone standing far too close.

The girl opened her eyes slowly. There was no dew on the windowpane. No thin steam coming from her mouth. She sat in silence for a long time, staring at her own palms. Turning them slowly as if to confirm they were indeed hers. Then, unconsciously, she reached for the side of the bed that was usually empty and cold. But that morning, even the empty space felt warm.
Instantly, the girl's body tensed.

The old house usually creaked when morning arrived. Its wood always made small sounds like an old person groaning softly. But this morning, the house was too quiet. Too still. As if something were listening. Then, from the floor below, a soft knocking came from the direction of the front door. The knocking sounded quiet, like fingernails tapping on wet wood. And the girl was certain, the woman had arrived exactly as promised.

Frantically, the girl pulled herself from the mattress and straightened her clothes. She opened the window, which blew in an uncanny warmth, looked down, and realized the woman had been looking up all along with a gentle smile, sorrowful eyes, and a graceful swing of her arm as if waving. The girl gave a silent nod and slowly closed the window again.
The wooden door opened, revealing the girl standing stiffly with a heavy tote bag in her hand.
"Hi, dear. Are you ready?" the woman greeted briefly. Her smile was now wider, stretching across her face in a way that felt forced.

"I am ready, but let me deliver this knitting to my neighbor," the girl replied hastily, though without waiting for a reply from the woman. The girl turned right, passing a few monotonous houses next to hers. But the woman remained silent and followed her slowly, soundlessly from behind.

The girl's footsteps creaked, breaking the morning silence, clashing against the dewy ground that was beginning to harden. However, no matter how hard she strained her ears, there was not a single sound of footsteps following her. The woman in the hat moved like a shadow—floating, sweeping across the street without leaving a trace, bringing with her a warm aura that uncannily made the hair on the girl's neck stand up.

Upon arriving in front of her neighbor's dull, stained wooden door, the girl knocked softly. The door creaked open, revealing the wrinkled face of the neighbor, who seemed to carry the exhaustion of the remaining night. However, that look of exhaustion vanished instantly, replaced by dilated pupils and a breath that suddenly caught. The old woman's gaze was not directed at the girl, but locked straight through her shoulder.
"The knitting is finished, Ma'am. As I promised," the girl said, breaking the awkwardness, handing over the neatly folded wool.

The neighbor did not respond immediately. Her suddenly trembling hand slowly reached for the knitting, while her eyes remained wide, staring at the graceful figure behind the girl. The air on the porch slowly felt suffocating, as if the oxygen was slowly being sucked out of their surroundings. With stiff, extremely hurried movements, the neighbor slipped a few coins into the girl's cold palm.
"Take this," the neighbor whispered, her voice hoarse and sounding almost like a whimper. Her fingers gripped the girl's wrist tightly for a moment. "And go... never look back while you walk."
The door was slammed shut instantly. The sound of a series of iron bars being pulled from the inside echoed, as if locking away a terror to keep it from entering her house.

The girl froze, staring at the coins in her hand—the last numbers she received, which for some reason now felt entirely worthless. She swallowed hard, remembering her neighbor's warning, but her instinct forced her to turn her head slowly.

The woman in the hat was still there. Only, the distance was now much closer than before, standing right in front of her until the girl could smell a nauseatingly sweet aroma. That forced smile was still plastered perfectly on her face, not shifting a single millimeter since she was in front of the house.
"Are you done saying goodbye to your numbers, dear?" she asked softly.
Strangely, the woman's lips did not move at all. That blanket-like voice no longer floated in the air, but echoed directly, heavy and suffocating, inside the girl's head.
With the girl now fully realizing that she was dealing with something far beyond human reason, which way would the woman in the hat lead her now?

The girl felt she had never walked this far. Her entire life, the map of her world was only the path to the market, the dead fields, and the frozen river. Now her tiny body was forced to drag a bag that felt increasingly heavy, in stark contrast to the woman in front of her. That figure stepped effortlessly, her heavy, layered clothes seeming to... flutter, as if she had her own wind.

Occasionally, the woman hummed. An uncanny melody the girl had never heard before. She also began to babble about how hard it was to find a girl like her—and what made the girl's stomach churn again was that the babbling voice still echoed softly inside her head, while viewed from behind, the woman's shoulders and posture remained motionless.
"I am sure you have met a fat man before," she said softly, echoing once again in the girl's ears.

The girl's steps faltered. Her shoes scraped softly against the frozen ground. Her stomach churned, reawakening the memory of the heavy, hot breath and the gaze from the man of fat the other day. Fear crept slowly up the back of her neck.
The woman stopped too, though her back remained turned to the girl. The wind instantly died, leaving a chest-crushing silence.

"His gaze was dirty and hungry, wasn't it?" the voice flowed softly again inside the girl's skull, smooth yet feeling as if it were flaying her. "Looking at you as if you were a piece of helpless fresh meat... or perhaps, an empty vessel he was free to fill with his rot. Whether he was merely a wretched man controlled by his feral lust, or something far more ancient and hungrier than that... his intentions were always equally vile."

The girl gripped her bag straps tightly until her knuckles turned white. The cold air she usually befriended now made her shiver. She began to realize that all this time, she hadn't just been poor; she was also being stalked, studied like lost prey.

"But it's only natural that many prey on you, dear," the echoing voice continued, its tone now softening, resembling the fake sympathy of someone admiring fragile porcelain. "You radiate a despair that is so pure. A young girl with hands that are always freezing, insisting on protecting memories that are slowly cracking. Something very appetizing to snatch away."
The girl swallowed the sharp lump in her throat. Her instinct screamed to drop her bag and run back to the village, but her feet felt as if they had taken root in the warm soil beneath her soles.

"But he was too noisy. Too vulgar," a small laugh followed, echoing inside the girl's head without vibrating the hat-wearing woman's shoulders at all. "I know you are not naive. You have a boundary regarding which despair you are willing to accept. That is why I didn't bother chasing that fatty creature away that day. Because from the start... I firmly believed, in the end, you would still come with me."

The woman finally turned around slowly. The shadow from the brim of her hat covered half her face, leaving a curved smile that now looked strained and far too wide—waiting for the girl to step forward and break the terrifying silence.

Without saying anything else, the woman raised one hand clad in a knitted glove, pointing forward. The girl swallowed the sharp lump in her throat, then gathered the courage to follow the direction of that index finger.
Her eyes slowly widened; her breath seemed forcefully pulled from her lungs.

The thick fog that had been obscuring their vision slowly parted, as if terrified by the existence of the woman's finger. Before them, the earth no longer lay flat. The map of the world the girl had known ended at this road. The ground ahead split to form a giant, perfectly circular ravine or pit—as if the world had a hole because something massive had just been plucked from there.

And at the bottom of that incredibly deep ravine, there was no snow. No frozen ice. There was only a majestic, looming structure made of pitch-black wood, distorted like a stilt house built upside down. The house stood silently in the middle of a sea of warm, slowly pulsating fog, waiting for its new occupant.

"Do you remember I promised a room at the bottom of my house?" the woman whispered. This time, the voice actually came from her own lips, breaking the absolute silence at the edge of that ravine. "Let us go down and meet your flame."

So the girl followed her down the stairs to the bottom of the house, so long and seemingly endless. The girl stumbled more and more, growing exhausted as she had to descend the stairs carrying a heavy bag. The woman glanced slightly to the right and muttered in a language the girl still couldn't understand. In an instant, her luggage felt light, as if she wasn't carrying anything. The girl still couldn't believe it and checked the contents of her bag. Which turned out to be completely intact, not missing a single thing; strangely, she was no longer surprised by the bizarre things before her. Deep in her heart, she believed that the one with her was not human.
The stone stairs stretched far too long. Far longer than a depth human logic could grasp, plunging through the fog until she began to doubt whether this ravine truly had a bottom.
"When will these stairs end?" the girl asked with an innocent, panting tone.
"Until you are ready, dear... oh, until you are ready," the woman replied, laughing slightly.
Time melted and rotted on those steps. The girl didn't know if they had been descending for hours, days, or just the span of one long breath.

At first, the girl's old habits took over. In silence, she began counting the steps in her head. A hundred and one, a hundred and two, fifteen hundred, who knows how many thousands. Rooted in her instinct, which was always faced with debts and measurable days. Every time she added a new number, the warm fog below them felt thicker, and the bottom of the ravine seemed to keep moving further away, mocking her efforts.

Ahead of her, the woman in the hat kept walking soundlessly, occasionally humming a tune that now sounded like the smoothed howling of the wind. Every beat of that hum seemed to strip a number from the girl's head. The more the girl tried to remember the amount of her mother's debt, the healers' bills, or the remaining coins in her hand—everything slowly blurred. Turning to ash.
Then, a realization struck the girl's chest, as cold as ice yet as clear as crystal.
*"Until you are ready..."*

Those words echoed again. As long as she kept counting steps, as long as she used numbers as the anchor of her rationality, these stairs would never touch the bottom. This world was not a world that could be measured. This was a world where memories and emotions were the sole currency.

So, taking a long, trembling breath, the girl stopped counting. She forced her head to discard the remaining coins, drown the rows of her mother's debts, and hold on to only one thing: the memory of her mother's warm breath on her hands every morning. She no longer cared which step she was on. She just walked, drowning in pure memory.
Right when the last number faded from her mind, the tip of her shoe hit something solid with a dull thud. No longer wooden planks, but black stone tiles gleaming with dew.
The girl opened her eyes wide. The stairs had ended.

They stood at the bottom of the ravine. The inverted stilt house structure now loomed right in front of her, pressing against the ceiling of fog with its dense and absolute aura. The tip of its roof was driven into the earth, while its foundation—which should have been on the ground—instead gripped the emptiness above. At the very bottom of that strange house was a carved oak door that looked centuries old.

The woman in the hat stepped to the side, no longer blocking the path. The girl turned and noticed a horrifying change. The forced smile that had stretched across the woman's face was now completely gone. Her face was blank, expressionless, lifeless. Her sorrowful gaze was now just two dark holes staring straight through the girl's soul, as if the essence that had been pretending to be human had now reverted to its apathetic, true form.

The oak door opened slowly without a sound, exhaling air that smelled like old books, frankincense, and something sweet yet charred. In the pitch-black darkness of the room, a few dozen paces inside, there was a beam of golden light pulsating weakly. Bright and dim. Bright and dim. Breathing.

"Go in," the woman's voice now sounded like thousands of dry leaves rustling against each other, no longer echoing in the girl's head, but whispering right in her ear. "Your flame is waiting for you. Keep it company. And remember..."
The woman leaned in slightly, her flat face now just a handspan away from the girl's.
"...do not let it sleep."
And with trembling steps, the girl entered the room. Behind the door of the windowless, soundless room, there was nothing but a small flame on a tiny pedestal in the center of the room.
"Why is it so quiet?" the girl asked, because in that room she could hear her own blood traveling, a soft rush like someone humming in the distance.

"So the flame is not disturbed," said the woman in the hat. "And so you never feel alone. Listen—the house is whispering to you, so you have a friend." She pointed to the flame. "As long as you love it, it will burn. Every time you love it, a little of your warmth transfers to it. That is love, dear. Love is always like that."

Then the woman stepped out. The wooden door closed without a sound. The girl now sat alone beside her small flame, staring at the dimly pulsating glow. And for the first time since her mother didn't wake up—deep within the crisscrossing paths of her confusion and fear—the girl felt useful.
The first winter arrived gently.

The girl didn't see it coming—there were no windows—but she felt it from the flame, which dimmed a little, just a fingernail's worth, as if sleepy. *Sleep, little flame,* the girl almost said, then remembered that was exactly what must not happen. So she inverted her mother's words. "Don't sleep, little flame," she whispered. "Let me keep watch." And she leaned in, loving that flame as hard as she could, and the flame grew bright again.

That morning—the girl called it morning, though there was no morning at the bottom of the house—she just felt that right after she woke up from sleep, it was morning. Her hands were colder than usual. But she didn't mind. She was used to befriending the cold. And didn't the woman in the hat say she would never be cold again? Surely she meant *later*. Surely the warmth would come later, after she proved herself, just as all good things always come later.

Strangely, her body seemed to understand that she was now in a world that no longer needed ordinary things. Days or perhaps weeks passed—she didn't know for sure—her stomach never whined to be filled. Her throat no longer demanded water. Even the urge to relieve herself simply evaporated. In that windowless room, she no longer felt entirely human; it was as if she were slowly turning into a lump of feeling whose only task was to sit, breathe, and guard.

The only human thing that occasionally came to greet her was an incredibly heavy drowsiness. At first, the girl was terrified. She squeezed her fingers tightly, bit her lip, and kept glaring at the flame. *Let me keep watch,* she whispered to herself, afraid that if she dozed off even for a second, the flame would die too. However, the silence of the room was too thick, stroking her head like an irresistible lullaby. In the end, she always surrendered. Her body slumped to the cold floor, and she fell into a dreamless sleep.

Then, every time she woke up from her long slumber, something had always changed in the corner of the room. Objects appeared silently, as if the room birthed them when she closed her eyes. Sometimes a cup of water or a piece of hard biscuit that strangely made her stomach feel full for days. But what appeared most often were stacks of old books with dull covers.

The girl had nothing else to do, so she read. The books contained strange tales from places she didn't know, yet their loneliness felt so close. She read about a little girl who kept swinging alone in a dead playground, waiting for a figure she thought was a friend when it was actually a monster. On another page, she found a story about a gloomy flower shop where someone arranged grief on paper. And there was also a story that made her ponder for a long time; about a desperate man digging empty graves near a cluster of blue flowers, searching for his lost wife.

Even on one slightly torn page, she found a description of a flabby, fat creature that wandered preying on human despair—making the girl shudder softly, remembering the heavy breath behind her door back then.

Besides that, sometimes those books contained stories or perhaps histories from a world she had never known. There were writings about eyeless creatures that ate the echoes of voices, about a civilization built upon the eyelids of a sleeping giant, and about ancient rituals where a human's shadow could be flayed. Reading those strange books became her new routine, distracting her mind from the absolute silence pressing against the stone walls. The dark stories inside those dusty pages somehow felt like they validated her sorrow, as if whispering to her that the world up there was indeed too broken to live in.

And every time she finished reading, she would return to her routine. Leaning in, loving the flame in front of her until it grew bright again, then pressing her hands together and starting to count to ensure she still existed.

She counted, to keep herself company. She counted not the hours, because there were no hours, but how many things she still remembered from up there. Her mother's face. The smell of rain on soil. The taste of salt. The name of the river near her house. She kept them like one keeps stars, and said to herself: *as long as I can still count them, I am still me.*
The third winter arrived without warning.

This time the flame did not dim a fingernail's worth, but almost half, and the girl had to lean in closer, had to love harder, had to give more. She gave the flame the name of the river near her house, because she thought maybe the flame would like having a name. When the flame grew bright again, the girl realized she could no longer remember the name of that river. She had given it. That was what giving meant.
*It's okay,* she told herself. *I still remember Mother's face. I still remember the smell of rain. I still have my stars. I still remember many things.*
